questions.problem: The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is
questions.worked_solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we plug $a=\frac{\pi }{4}$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(\frac{\pi }{4})+{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}){(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ and ${f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(x) & ⟹ &  & f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x)} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{{cos}^{3}⁡(x)} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =4\end{aligned}
$$

We now plug the results for $f(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ and ${f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =1+2(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+4\cdot \frac{1}{2}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2} \\  & =1+2(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+2{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Coefficient in a Second-Degree Taylor Polynomial
questions.problem: What is the coefficient of ${(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}$ in the second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =f(\frac{\pi }{4})+{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}){(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of ${(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}$ in the above Taylor polynomial is 

$$
\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}).
$$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of ${(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What is the coefficient of $(x-\pi )^{2}$ in the second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ at $x=\pi ?$
questions.worked_solution:
The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=\pi $ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =f(\pi )+{f}^{′}(\pi )(x-\pi )+\frac{{f}^{″}(\pi )}{2}(x-\pi )^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of $(x-\pi )^{2}$ in the above Taylor polynomial is 

$$
\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\pi ).
$$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=\pi .$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}(\pi )=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )=-(-1)=1.
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of $(x-\pi )^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{″}(\pi )}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What is the coefficient of $(x-1)^{2}$ in the second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-{x}^{3}}$ at $x=1?$
questions.worked_solution:
The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =f(1)+{f}^{′}(1)(x-1)+\frac{{f}^{″}(1)}{2}(x-1)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of $(x-1)^{2}$ in the above Taylor polynomial is

$$
\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(1).
$$

$$

$$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-{x}^{3}} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-{x}^{2}{e}^{-{x}^{3}} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-2x{e}^{-{x}^{3}}+3{x}^{4}{e}^{-{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1) & =-2\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{-{1}^{3}}+3\cdot {1}^{4}\cdot {e}^{-{1}^{3}} \\  & =-2{e}^{-1}+3{e}^{-1} \\  & ={e}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of $(x-1)^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{″}(1)}{2} & =\frac{{e}^{-1}}{2}=\frac{1}{2e}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the second-degree Taylor polynomial ${P}_{2}(x)$ of $f(x)=\frac{1}{1-\sqrt{2}\,x}$ about $x=0.$

${P}_{2}(x)=$
{{field-1}}$\,+$
{{field-2}}$\,x\,+$
{{field-3}}$\,{x}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)(x-0)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(0)(x-0)^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ and ${f}^{″}(0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{1-\sqrt{2}\,x}=(1-\sqrt{2}\,x)^{-1} & ⟹ &  & f(0) & =1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\sqrt{2}(1-\sqrt{2}\,x)^{-2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(0) & =\sqrt{2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =4(1-\sqrt{2}\,x)^{-3} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(0) & =4\end{aligned}
$$

We now plug the results for $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ and ${f}^{″}(0)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =1+\sqrt{2}\,x+4\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2} \\  & =1+\sqrt{2}\,x+2\,{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
